analysis.one_liner: Caps federal prison commissary prices at normal retail and bans vendor kickback contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors and no action since its introduction on July 23, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal Bureau of Prisons to price commissary goods—soap, food, phone items, and other basics that incarcerated people and their families buy—at no more than what the same items cost at ordinary retail stores in that state. It would force competitive bidding for commissary contracts and ban contracts that include revenue-sharing, the arrangement in which a prison system takes a cut of commissary sales. It would also require monthly price reviews, an annual public report, and a yearly audit.
analysis.who_benefits: People incarcerated in federal prisons and their families, who currently pay inflated prices for basics from a market where they have no choice of seller. By banning revenue-sharing contracts, the bill also removes an incentive for prison systems to keep prices high in order to collect a bigger cut.

how_it_helps.text: Caps commissary prices at fair market value, defined as the average retail price at ordinary stores in the state, while explicitly excluding prices charged by prisons and other captive markets from the calculation [S2].

Bans revenue-sharing in commissary contracts, the practice under which the Bureau of Prisons or other agencies take a share of commissary revenue that is otherwise recovered through higher prices [S2].

Requires competitive bidding for commissary contracts, monthly price reviews, an annual public report of prices and contract terms for each facility, and an annual Government Accountability Office-style audit by the Comptroller General [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Commissary vendors, who lose their pricing power over a captive customer base and the ability to bid for contracts padded to cover revenue-sharing payments. The Bureau of Prisons may also collect less commissary revenue, which it has historically used to help fund inmate programs, so those programs could take a budget hit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commissary vendors and federal prison budgets

drawbacks.text: Federal prison commissary profits have traditionally helped fund inmate programs and amenities; capping prices could leave a funding hole for those programs unless Congress appropriates money to replace it [S2].
The bill covers only federal Bureau of Prisons facilities, leaving the same pricing and kickback practices untouched in the far larger population held in state and county jails and prisons [S2].
Requiring monthly nationwide price reviews for every commissary good would impose a continuous administrative burden on an agency without new funding for the work [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and direct: it lowers the price of everyday basics for a group of consumers with no alternative seller and removes a built-in financial incentive for the government itself to overcharge them. The main costs are reduced commissary revenue that some inmate programs rely on and a heavy monthly compliance workload. A fair reading is that the bill targets a genuine pricing problem but should be paired with replacement funding for the programs commissary margins currently support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no committee action since July 23, 2026 [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Valerie Foushee introduced the Stop Prison Price Gouging Act of 2026 in the House on July 23, 2026 [S1][S2].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and no further action has been taken [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commissary vendors and the federal prison commissary revenue stream remain untouched, since no pricing cap or contract rule has been adopted.

for.name: Rep. Valerie Foushee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill—no markup, hearing, or floor recommendation—since it was referred

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes, so there is no record of where either party stands.

industries.note: These companies sell into a market where customers cannot shop elsewhere, and contracts can be padded to cover revenue-sharing payments to the prison system. The bill caps their prices at ordinary retail levels and bans the kickback structure, cutting into their margins.

industries.industry: Bureau of Prisons commissary revenue fund
industries.note: The federal prison system collects a share of commissary sales, which historically helps fund inmate programs and facilities. Capping prices and ending revenue-sharing shrinks that revenue, which helps buyers but could reduce program funding.

analysis.trajectory: A solo-sponsored bill with no cosponsors, introduced in late July of the second session and referred to a committee that has taken no action, rarely advances to a markup or floor vote before the Congress ends in January 2027.
